title: Protect me with your hand
hook: hamree karo hath dai rachhaa: give me Your hand and keep me safe (Chaupai)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benti Chaupai, and your line, shelter me. This week the drums faded, the crane was found out, the secret was love, those who loved found, the ten savaiye closed, and a quiet prayer began. Today, its first line.

In Punjabi, there's an old way of saying I'll stand by you: I've taken your arm. It's a promise, the kind you don't walk away from. It's what a family does for a newcomer, an elder for a frightened child, a friend when your life falls apart. Not a handshake. A grip. And it's the first picture in the Tenth Guru's prayer for protection, the very first thing it asks for.
screen: `I'VE TAKEN YOUR ARM.` → `NOT A HANDSHAKE. A GRIP.` → `THE PRAYER'S FIRST PICTURE.`

segments.voice: The line is hamree karo haath dai rachhaa. Hamree: mine, our. Karo: make, do. Haath dai: giving your hand. Rachhaa: protection, guarding. Protect me, giving me your hand. Rachhaa is the poem's form of raksha, protection, the word also used for protective threads and amulets. But the line asks for something else: a hand. Not an object to carry around, but the protector, reaching in. The Guru isn't asking for a charm; he's asking to be held. Sikh teaching often points away from charms like these and toward the One, directly. Why a hand? Because a hand is personal. An army can protect you. A wall can protect you. But only someone right there, close enough to touch, can give you their hand. The line asks God to be that near. And it asks it of someone who sees everything, as later lines say, so it isn't a request to be noticed. It's a request to be held, while noticed. Near its close, this same prayer returns to the picture from the hook: the one who has taken my arm. We'll get there on day three hundred seventy-eight. For now, just the first line. Hamree karo haath dai rachhaa. Keep me by the hand.
screen: `HAMREE KARO HAATH DAI RACHHAA.` · `RACHHAA: RAKSHA, PROTECTION.` · `NOT A CHARM, BUT A HAND.` · `A HAND MEANS SOMEONE NEAR.` · then, large: `KEEP ME BY THE HAND.`

segments.voice: Place one hand flat on the center of your chest and feel its warmth and weight, and the heartbeat or the breath underneath. Let the hand do what a hand does: steady you. If you pray, say the line, hamree karo haath dai rachhaa, or simply Waheguru; if not, let yourself be held for a minute, even by your own hand.
Rachhaa, protection. Hamree karo haath dai rachhaa: the first line of Chaupai, asking not for a charm but for a hand, someone near enough to hold you.
Your line: keep me by the hand. Not a charm, a hand. That's one line; more tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this opening line of Chaupai Sahib each morning and evening, and some say it on its own as a short prayer before a journey or a difficult moment.

notes: Week-end look-back (days 365–371) is in the review.
Transliteration 'hamree karo haath dai rachhaa' (the index writes 'hamree karo hath dai rachhaa'); confirm preferred spelling.

Rachhaa from Sanskrit raksha, and the link to protective threads/amulets: confirm. The line 'the tradition consistently turns away from protective objects as magic' summarizes Sikh teaching against amulets and charms; confirm phrasing.
The Punjabi idiom of 'taking someone's arm' (baanh pharna) as a promise of protection, and its echo in the closing dohra (baanh gahe kee laaj): confirm.
Original: ਹਮਰੀ ਕਰੋ ਹਾਥ ਦੈ ਰੱਛਾ; standard texts may print ਰਛਾ. Confirm spelling.
